seoTitle: Unix Timestamp Converter - Epoch to Date
metaDescription: Easily convert Unix timestamps to human-readable dates and vice versa. Instantly view current Epoch time, seconds, and milliseconds.
intro: Need to translate a 10-digit machine timestamp into a human-readable date, or vice versa? The Unix Timestamp Converter makes it incredibly easy to switch between Epoch time and standard dates instantly. Whether you are debugging database records, testing API responses, analyzing server logs, or just trying to figure out exactly when a system event occurred, this tool provides instant, bidirectional translation between raw Unix time and perfectly formatted local and GMT dates.
whatIs: The Unix Timestamp Converter is a specialized developer utility that translates Unix Epoch time—which is the total number of seconds that have elapsed since midnight Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) on January 1, 1970—into human-readable dates, and vice versa. While machines and databases prefer the efficiency of storing time as a single integer, humans need standard calendar formats. This tool acts as the bridge, seamlessly handling the complex math of leap years and varying month lengths to give you an accurate translation instantly.
howToUse: Step 1: To convert an existing timestamp, type or paste the integer (either 10 digits for seconds or 13 digits for milliseconds) into the 'Timestamp to Date' input box.
Step 2: The tool will instantly process the integer and display the corresponding date in both GMT/UTC and your local time zone.
Step 3: To convert a human date into a timestamp, use the 'Date to Timestamp' section to select your desired year, month, day, and time.
Step 4: The calculator will immediately generate the corresponding Unix integer.
Step 5: Use the 'Current Epoch Time' button to instantly grab the exact timestamp of the current moment.
howItWorks: Unix time represents the absolute number of seconds (or milliseconds) since the Unix Epoch (1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC). The tool applies native JavaScript date parsing algorithms to instantly translate this integer. It calculates the exact number of days, accounts for leap years, and determines the time of day. It then outputs this information twice: once aligned strictly to GMT/UTC, and once adjusted by the specific timezone offset of the browser you are currently using.
workedExample: Suppose you are reviewing a database log and see the timestamp 1711234567. You paste this into the converter. The tool instantly calculates the time elapsed since Jan 1, 1970. It outputs 'Sat, 23 Mar 2024 22:56:07 GMT'. Furthermore, if you are located in New York (Eastern Standard Time, typically UTC-4 or UTC-5 depending on Daylight Saving), the tool will automatically apply the offset and also display the local equivalent, such as 'Sat, 23 Mar 2024 18:56:07 EDT'.
resultInterpretation: The converter clearly outputs the resulting date in two distinct formats to prevent any confusion: GMT (Greenwich Mean Time / UTC) and your Local Time based on your device's settings. It also explicitly shows the format (e.g., MM/DD/YYYY, HH:MM:SS) so you know exactly what you are reading. When converting from a date to a timestamp, the result is provided as a simple, easily copyable integer string.
useCases: Database Debugging: Translating raw integer timestamps stored in MySQL, PostgreSQL, or MongoDB into readable dates to track down exactly when a user registered or an error occurred.
API Development: Verifying JSON payloads that use Epoch time to ensure your backend is sending the correct temporal data to the frontend.
Log Analysis: Reading and parsing server logs that track system events by the second, allowing system administrators to pinpoint the exact moment of a server crash or traffic spike.
Software Testing: Generating specific past or future Unix timestamps to test how an application handles date-based edge cases, like expiring tokens or scheduled events.
tipsAndLimitations: Tip: The tool safely handles timestamps in both seconds (typically 10 digits) and milliseconds (typically 13 digits). It will automatically attempt to detect which format you pasted.
Tip: Keep in mind that Unix time does not care about time zones; the integer is exactly the same everywhere in the world. Only the human translation changes based on location.
Limitation: Standard Unix time does not directly count leap seconds; every day is treated mathematically as exactly 86400 seconds.

faq.question: What is the Year 2038 Problem?
faq.answer: The Year 2038 problem (often called the Y2K38 bug) occurs because older 32-bit computing systems will run out of integer space to store the Unix timestamp on January 19, 2038, causing the integer to overflow into negative numbers. This specific online tool uses 64-bit JavaScript numbers, so it is completely immune to the 2038 problem and can calculate dates far into the future.

faq.question: Why does my timestamp show the wrong year, like 1970 or 54,000?
faq.answer: You are likely entering milliseconds into an input field that expects seconds, or vice versa. For example, if you enter a 13-digit millisecond timestamp into a system interpreting it as seconds, the date will be thousands of years in the future. The tool tries to auto-detect this, but always verify the digit length (10 vs 13).

faq.question: Is Unix time affected by Daylight Saving Time?
faq.answer: No. The Unix timestamp itself is an absolute measure of time since 1970 and is completely unaffected by Daylight Saving Time. Only the local translation of that timestamp changes when DST begins or ends.
